skill_title: State Newton's laws, draw free-body diagrams and apply Fnet = ma to a single body

items.question: What does Newton's First Law state?
items.expectedAnswer: A body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a non-zero net force.
items.explanation: Newton's First Law (inertia): no net force means no change in motion.
options: A body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a non-zero net force.
Force equals mass times acceleration.
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

items.question: What does Newton's Second Law state?
items.expectedAnswer: The net force equals mass times acceleration (Fnet = ma).
items.explanation: Newton's Second Law: Fnet = ma, acceleration in the direction of the net force.
options: A body at rest stays at rest.
The net force equals mass times acceleration (Fnet = ma).
Forces always occur in pairs.

items.question: What does Newton's Third Law state?
items.expectedAnswer: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on a different body.
items.explanation: Newton's Third Law: action–reaction pairs are equal, opposite, and act on different objects.
options: A body keeps moving at constant velocity.
Net force equals mass times acceleration.
For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on a different body.

items.question: A free-body diagram shows...
items.expectedAnswer: all the forces acting ON one chosen object.
items.explanation: A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on the single chosen body.
options: all the forces acting ON one chosen object.
the forces the object exerts on other things.
the velocity and position of the object.

items.question: A 5 kg object experiences a net force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
items.explanation: Fnet = ma ⇒ a = Fnet/m = 10/5 = 2 m·s⁻².

items.question: What is the weight of a 4 kg object? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
items.explanation: Weight = mg = 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N.

items.question: An object moves at constant velocity. What is the net force on it?
items.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Fnet = ma the net force is zero.

items.question: Which is an example of a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.expectedAnswer: A swimmer pushes water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
items.explanation: Action–reaction pairs act on different bodies: swimmer on water, water on swimmer.
options: The weight of a book and the normal force on it.
A swimmer pushes water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
Friction and the applied force on a box.

items.question: A 2 kg trolley accelerates at 3 m·s⁻². What net force acts on it?
items.explanation: Fnet = ma = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

items.question: Why is the weight and the normal force on a book on a table NOT a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.expectedAnswer: They act on the same body (the book), not on two different bodies.
items.explanation: Third Law pairs act on different objects; weight and normal force both act on the book.
options: They act on the same body (the book), not on two different bodies.
They are not equal in size.
They act in the same direction.

items.question: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 2.5 m·s⁻². What net force is needed?
A 10 kg box is pushed with 50 N forward while 20 N of friction opposes it. What is its acceleration?
A 3 kg object on a frictionless floor is pulled with a horizontal force of 12 N. What is its acceleration?
items.explanation: No friction, so Fnet = 12 N; a = 12/3 = 4 m·s⁻².

items.question: A 6 kg object is lifted by a rope with a tension of 70 N. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
Why does a passenger lurch forward when a bus suddenly brakes?
items.expectedAnswer: Inertia — the passenger tends to keep moving (Newton's First Law).
items.explanation: By inertia (First Law), the body keeps moving forward when the bus decelerates.
options: A force pushes them forward.
Gravity increases during braking.
Inertia — the passenger tends to keep moving (Newton's First Law).

items.question: A net force of 24 N gives an object an acceleration of 6 m·s⁻². What is the object's mass?
items.explanation: Fnet = ma ⇒ m = Fnet/a = 24/6 = 4 kg.

items.question: On the free-body diagram of a box resting on the floor, which forces act?
items.explanation: Forces ON the box: its weight down and the normal force up; the box's push on the floor is not on the box.
options: Weight only.
Weight (down) and normal force (up).
Normal force and the force of the box on the floor.

items.question: A 0.5 kg ball in free fall (ignoring air resistance) has what net force on it? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
items.explanation: The only force is weight: Fnet = mg = 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 N downward.

items.question: A 4 kg object is pushed with 30 N but does not move. What is the friction force on it?
items.explanation: Not moving ⇒ zero acceleration ⇒ net force zero, so static friction balances the push: 30 N.

items.question: Two forces act on a 5 kg object: 40 N right and 15 N left. What is its acceleration?
items.explanation: Fnet = 40 − 15 = 25 N right; a = 25/5 = 5 m·s⁻².
